To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the prevalence of human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection among the general population of the United States is low and that the prevalence among high-risk populations such as intravenous drug users (IDUs) and homosexuals is high.

(a) the current US epidemic has been fueled by the spread of HIV from high-risk groups to the general population and that (b) the epidemic in Africa and elsewhere in the developing world has been fueled by heterosexual transmission.
the HIV/AIDS epidemic has become global, and the United States is not isolated from the epidemic.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a new class of materials that can be used as a substrate for the immobilization of enzymes.
the development of new and more efficient methods for solving a wide range of problems arising in the mathematical sciences.
understanding the nature of the HIV epidemic and how it is changing.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the HIV/AIDS pandemic is a global phenomenon and that the US is not immune.
US physicians must be cognizant of the international spread and dynamics of HIV infection.

US physicians should care deeply about HIV/AIDS in the global village for the following reasons: (1) the HIV/AIDS pandemic has become a major international health problem; (2) HIV/AIDS is a global problem that is affecting all countries and all populations; (3) HIV/AIDS has the potential to become a serious public health problem in the US; and (4) US physicians have the opportunity and responsibility to be involved in the fight against HIV/AIDS worldwide.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the US is a global community and as such we are all affected by HIV/AIDS.
HIV infection and AIDS have become global phenomena and that US physicians should be concerned about them in the same way they are concerned about the spread of tuberculosis.
the US is not immune from what is happening in the rest of the world.
The main takeaway from our work is that
HIV is not a disease of the past and is not limited to the US.
the US must not be complacent in the fight against HIV/AIDS and should not ignore the lessons learned from the HIV epidemics in Africa and other parts of the developing world.
HIV is not a disease of the poor or the rich of the black or the white of the gay or the straight.
